v1.text: Furniture. Luggage. Gold. Rice. Knowledge. Work. We’re told to memorise lists like these: no plural, singular verb.
But what if you didn’t have to memorise them? What if you could prove it, with logic?
Case one: furniture. Why is ‘The furniture are expensive’ wrong?
Proof one. Point to a furniture. This? That’s a chair. This? A table. A sofa. A bed. Every object already has its own name.
Nothing here is ‘a furniture’. So furniture is not the name of one object.
Proof two. Furniture is the name for the whole group. Chair, table, sofa, bed: one box, one label.
Try counting the label: one furniture, two furnitures? It fails. We count what’s inside: one chair, two chairs.
Proof three. A group name works as one whole, so the verb is singular: ‘The furniture is expensive.’
Need a number? The two won’t stick to furniture. Give it something countable: ‘Two pieces of furniture are expensive.’
Now you try: luggage. Point to a luggage? No, that’s a suitcase, that’s a bag. Group name, so: ‘The luggage is heavy.’
So don’t memorise. Ask: can I point to one of it? If not, it’s a group name. Treat it as one.

v2.text: A ring. A coin. A necklace. Three golden things. Now watch: melt them down. How many golds do you have now?
Three? One? The question doesn’t even work. And that’s the whole lesson, with no memorising.
Case two: materials. Why do we say ‘made of gold’, and never ‘made of golds’?
Proof one: the cut test. Cut a ring in half. Is it still a ring? No. It’s a broken ring.
Now cut a lump of gold in half. Still gold? Yes. Cut it again. Still gold. However small, it’s still gold.
Proof two. So how do we give a number? Count the objects: three rings. Or measure the material: twenty grams of gold. The number never lands on gold.
Proof three, the twist. Bricks can be counted: this wall has forty bricks. But brick is also a material, like gold.
So both are right. ‘Made of bricks’ means the blocks. ‘Made of brick’ means the material. The meaning decides the grammar.
Your turn: wood. Cut a plank in half. Still wood? Yes. So: ‘This table is made of wood.’
So don’t memorise. Cut it in half. If every piece is still the same stuff, it’s a material. Measure it, don’t count it.

sm.text: Why is ‘The furniture are expensive’ wrong?
Look at what furniture contains: a chair, a table, a sofa, a bed. Many different things.
But English doesn’t name each one. It groups them together and names them as one unit: furniture.
Why? Because furniture is not the name of an object. It’s the name of the whole collection. The word comes from ‘furnish’: everything you furnish a room with.
And a unit means one. One is always singular. We can’t add s to one. So: ‘The furniture is expensive.’
The same logic works for the whole family. Luggage: bags and suitcases. Equipment: tools and machines. Clothing: shirts and trousers. Crockery: plates and cups. Stationery: pens and paper.
Notice the endings: luggage, equipment, clothing, crockery. These endings often build a word for a whole collection.
So each one is one unit, with a singular verb: the luggage is heavy, the equipment is new, my clothing is wet.
Need to count them? Count a piece: two pieces of furniture, three pieces of luggage, an item of clothing.
So don’t memorise the list. See the unit: many things, one name, one verb.

rf.text: Quick question. Why do we never say furnitures, equipments, or luggages?
Now the room has furniture. Not three furnitures. Just furniture.
English doesn’t name each piece. It groups them into one unit. And a unit means one. One is always singular, so no s: the furniture is new.
Now a mechanic’s workshop, and an empty toolbox.
Close the lid. Many tools, one box, one unit: equipment. So: the equipment is ready.
Now someone is getting ready for the airport.
Bags and suitcases together make one unit: luggage. So: my luggage is heavy.
Need a number? Count a piece: two pieces of furniture, a piece of equipment, three pieces of luggage.
So don’t memorise the list. See the unit: many things, one name, one verb.

wb.text: Look at this sentence: ‘The furniture are expensive.’ It sounds fine, but it’s wrong. Let’s find out why, with logic, not memorising.
Here is the idea. Some nouns don’t name one single thing. They name a whole group of things, and the group acts as one unit.
Let’s see it. Here is a chair. Here is a table. A sofa. And a bed.
Four different things. But English doesn’t use four names here. It draws a circle around them, and gives the whole group one name: furniture.
So furniture is not one object. It is one unit. And a unit means one.
One is always singular. We can’t add s to one. So there is no ‘furnitures’, and the verb must be singular too.
So the correct sentence is: ‘The furniture is expensive.’
Let’s prove it again. A plate. A bowl. A mug. Circle them, and name the group: crockery. One unit, so: ‘The crockery is clean.’ Never ‘crockeries’.
One more. A fork. A knife. A spoon. Circle them: cutlery. One unit, so: ‘The cutlery is in the drawer.’
And if you need a number? Count the pieces, not the unit: two pieces of furniture, a piece of cutlery.
So remember the logic: many things, one circle, one unit, one name, one singular verb. That’s error one.

ul.text: Uncountable nouns. Why can’t we add s to them? And why can’t they take a plural verb?
Countable nouns are easy: a chair, two chairs, three ideas. We count them one by one, so they can take s.
But what about water, rice, honesty, or music? Nobody says two waters, or three honesties.
Most books just give you a list to memorise. We won’t. We’ll use logic. Uncountable nouns fall into five categories, and each category has its own reason.
One: unit, or mass. Two: material. Three: measured. Four: abstract. And five: activity, or process.
Let’s prove them one at a time.
Error one. ‘Furniture are expensive.’ That’s wrong. The correct sentence is: ‘Furniture is expensive.’ But why?
Category one: unit, or mass. This kind of noun is a unit, and a unit contains many things.
Look. A chair. A table. A bed. A sofa. A desk. Many individual things.
English groups them together. It draws one circle around them, and treats the whole group as one unit, called furniture.
And a unit means one. The whole group now works as one thing: one. And we can’t add s to one.
One is always singular. So the word stays singular, and so does the verb.
But why is furniture one unit? Because furniture is not the name of one object. It’s the name of the whole collection. The word comes from ‘furnish’: everything you furnish a room with.
So the correct sentence is: ‘The furniture is expensive.’

The old school rule says: furniture, luggage, baggage and crockery are always singular. Memorise it. Skip that. Here’s the logic: many individual things are named as one unit. Unit means one, and one is always singular.
The same logic works everywhere. Luggage: bags and suitcases together, one whole. Clothing: shirts and trousers, one category. Crockery: plates and cups, one collection.
And if you need a number, count a piece: a piece of furniture, a piece of luggage, an item of clothing.
Now think about it. Why can you say ‘two chairs’, but not ‘two rice’?
Error two. ‘This ring is made of golds.’ Wrong. ‘This ring is made of gold.’
Category two: material. A material is what something is made from. It’s a substance.
Take gold. It’s a substance, and it’s used to make many different things: a ring, a coin, a crown.
We can count the things: one ring, two coins. But the substance itself is measured, not counted. We weigh gold in grams.
So a material noun, used as a material, isn’t made plural. ‘This ring is made of gold.’

The old school rule says: brick, sand, milk, glass and water are always singular. Memorise it. Skip that. The logic: it’s the material used to make other things, so you measure it rather than count it.
Silver: used for jewellery, measured, not counted. Wood: used for furniture, measured in cubic metres. Water: used for drinking, measured in litres.
One careful note. When you mean separate objects, you can count them: a wall made of bricks, or two glasses of water. But as a material, it’s brick and glass, with no s.
Now think about it. Do we say ‘one milk’, or ‘one litre of milk’?
Error three. ‘I ate too many rice for lunch.’ Wrong. ‘I ate too much rice for lunch.’
Category three: measured. Food and substances like rice are measured by amount, not counted as separate items.
Rice comes as many tiny grains. We don’t count them one by one. We measure the amount instead: a cup of rice, a kilo of rice, a plate of rice.
Measured, not counted, so it always takes a singular verb. ‘This rice is delicious.’

Material and food nouns can look alike, so here’s the test: do we buy it in a measured amount, like a kilo or a litre, and not in pieces? If yes, it’s uncountable. The old school rule says food, meat, sugar, salt, tea and bread are always singular. The logic: they’re measured, not counted.
Bread: measured in loaves or slices. Milk: measured in litres. Salt: measured by weight.
Now think about it. Can you say ‘two rice’, or do you need to say ‘two kilos of rice’?
Error four. ‘He has many knowledges about art.’ Wrong. ‘He has a lot of knowledge about art.’
Category four: abstract. An abstract noun has no physical form. It can’t be held or touched.
It’s an idea, a quality, or a state. Knowledge, honesty, advice, happiness. You can’t put them on a table and count them.
You experience it, show it, or possess it, but you never count it. So it’s singular: ‘Her knowledge is impressive.’

The old school rule says advice, information, evidence and knowledge are always singular. Skip that. The logic: we can’t physically hold them, or count them directly. Need a number? A piece of advice, a piece of information, a piece of evidence.
Now think about it. Can you hold honesty in your hand, or can you only show it, have it, or experience it?
Error five. ‘She does many works every day.’ Wrong. ‘She does a lot of work every day.’
Category five: activity, or process. We talk about an ongoing process as a whole, not as separate actions.

Think about what work means. Work is many small steps: answering emails, making calls, going to meetings, writing reports. We don’t count each step. We put one circle around all of them, and call the whole activity: work.
Research is the same. Reading, asking questions, collecting data, testing, and writing up the results. Many steps, one circle, one process: research.
One process, not separate actions, so a singular verb. ‘Her research is impressive.’
The old school rule says work, research, progress, travel and exercise are always singular. Skip that. The logic: you’re talking about the whole activity, not separate actions.

The same goes for the whole family. Work: the whole activity of working. Research: the whole process of studying. Progress: the process of improving. Travel: going from place to place. Exercise: physical training in general. Training: developing a skill. Sleep: the state of sleeping. Shopping: buying things. And business: buying, selling and trading.
Now think about it. Do we say ‘I do a work’, or ‘I do work’?
So here’s the crux. How do you know a noun is uncountable? Check five things.
Does it work as one unit? Pens, pencils, clips and a ruler: circle them, and they’re stationery.
Is it a material? A house made of stone.
Is it usually measured rather than counted? A jar of honey.
Is it abstract, with no physical form? Peace.
Or is it an activity, taken as a whole? Exercise.
If the answer is yes, it’s uncountable: no s, and a singular verb.
Let’s put all the examples on the board.
Unit or mass: furniture, luggage, baggage, equipment, machinery, garbage, rubbish, clothing, stationery, crockery, cutlery, scenery and traffic. Many things, one unit.
Material: gold, silver, iron, copper, steel, wood, stone, sand, clay, cotton, wool, silk, leather, plastic, glass and paper. It’s what things are made of.
Measured: food, rice, bread, butter, cheese, meat, sugar, flour, salt, milk, water, tea, coffee and honey. Measured by amount.
Abstract: advice, information, knowledge, education, honesty, justice, patience, courage, wisdom, happiness, freedom, peace and evidence. No physical form.
Activity or process: work, research, progress, travel, exercise, training, sleep, shopping and business. One whole activity.
So don’t memorise the list. Find the category, and the logic tells you: no s, and a singular verb. That’s the Grammar Logic Series.
